t: The word republic comes from the Latin res publica, “public thing”, the government Rome adopted after expelling its kings in the 6th century BCE; Polybius praised it as a mixture of monarchy, aristocracy and democracy.

Republicanism holds that sovereignty resides in the people and stresses civic virtue, the common good and the fight against corruption; modern scholars see it as a stream distinct from liberalism, which rests on economics and individualism.

Revived in the trading city-states of late medieval and Renaissance Europe, it shaped the English Commonwealth, the American and French Revolutions and Latin American independence; today a republic usually means a democracy with an elected head of state.
dyk: Pasquale Paoli’s Corsican Republic (1755–1769) is thought to have had the first constitution in the world to give women the vote, to female heads of family; Rousseau wrote that “some day that little island will astonish Europe”, and five American counties are named Paoli.
ev: Lucius Junius Brutus and Collatinus expel the kings from Rome, and the res publica takes their place
After the overthrow of Charles I, Oliver Cromwell sets up the Commonwealth of England, which lasts until 1660
Pasquale Paoli’s Corsican Republic, the first Enlightenment republic in Europe, introduces universal male suffrage
The American Revolution, driven by republican values, breaks with Britain
Revolutionaries overthrow the French monarchy and found the First French Republic
In exile in Marseille, Giuseppe Mazzini founds Young Italy to make Italy a unitary democratic republic
Mustafa Kemal Atatürk leads the declaration of the Republic of Turkey
A referendum on 2 June makes Italy a republic, the first republican rule over the whole peninsula since ancient Rome

f.thinkers: Polybius and Cicero, of the mixed constitution of Rome; Niccolò Machiavelli, author of the period’s key work on republics; James Harrington and John Milton, of the English Commonwealth; Montesquieu and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, of the Enlightenment; John Adams and James Madison, American founders; Giuseppe Mazzini, who revived the republican idea in Italy; Philip Pettit, theorist of neo-republicanism
f.texts: Plato, The Republic; Cicero, De re publica; Niccolò Machiavelli, Discourses on Livy; Jean Bodin, Six Books of the Commonwealth (1576); Jean-Jacques Rousseau, On the Social Contract (1762); James Boswell, An Account of Corsica; John Adams, A Defense of the Constitutions of Government of the United States of America; James Madison, Federalist No. 10; J. G. A. Pocock, The Machiavellian Moment (1975)
f.ideas: sovereignty of the people and their elected representatives; civic virtue and active participation; the common good; a balanced and mixed constitution; government limited by constitutional law and the rule of law; freedom as non-domination; the fight against corruption; rejection of hereditary monarchy and aristocracy
f.today: a republic now usually means a representative democracy with an elected head of state serving a limited term; foundational to the constitution of the United States; one of the six principles of Kemalism in Turkey; the Italian Republican Party, founded in 1895, is Italy’s oldest active party; republican movements in monarchies such as Britain and Spain; the neo-republican scholarship of Philip Pettit, Cass Sunstein and Michael Sandel
